title: URL Patterns and Routing
description: Map URLs to views using `urlpatterns` and `path()`.

slides.title: URL Dispatcher 📍
slides.content:
Django uses a **URL dispatcher** to match incoming requests to views. It's defined in the project's `urls.py` and optionally in app‑level `urls.py` files.

The `urlpatterns` list contains `path()` objects that specify a route and the view to call.

slides.title: Basic URL Configuration
slides.codeSnippet:
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path
from myapp import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('admin/', admin.site.urls),
    path('', views.home, name='home'),
]

slides.title: How Matching Works 🔎
slides.content: When a request comes in, Django goes through `urlpatterns` in order. The first pattern that matches the request URL (after stripping domain and GET parameters) is used. The matching view is called, and if no match is found, Django returns a 404 error.

quizData.question: What happens if no URL pattern matches the request?

options.text: Django redirects to the home page

quizData.explanation: If no pattern matches, Django sends a 404 (Not Found) response.

slides.title: Including App URLs
slides.content: To keep things modular, you can include app‑level URLconfs:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Project urls.py
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    path('blog/', include('blog.urls')),
]

# Inside blog/urls.py
from django.urls import path
from . import views

urlpatterns = [
    path('', views.post_list, name='post_list'),
    path('<int:post_id>/', views.post_detail, name='post_detail'),
]

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Name your URLs

Always provide a `name` parameter in `path()`. It allows you to refer to URLs by name in templates and views, making your code more maintainable.
